comma_castle.q:
Choose the correct version:
“My brother a talented pianist won the regional contest.”
opts: My brother, a talented pianist, won
My brother a talented pianist, won
My brother, a talented pianist won
comma_castle.why: An appositive (“a talented pianist”) is extra info — it needs a PAIR of commas, one on each side.

comma_castle.q:
Pick the correctly punctuated list:
“She packed apples pears and plums for the hike.”
comma_castle.why: Items in a series take commas between them. The ACT accepts the Oxford comma — and it never hurts.

comma_castle.q:
Which fixes the comma splice?
“The test was long, I still finished early.”
comma_castle.why: Two complete sentences cannot be glued with just a comma. A semicolon, a period, or a comma + FANBOYS fixes it.

comma_castle.q: Which sentence punctuates the city and its country correctly?
opts: We visited Paris, France, in May.
We visited Paris France in May.
We visited Paris, France in May.
We visited, Paris France, in May.
comma_castle.why: City, country needs commas around the country name — it is a paired appositive like any other.

comma_castle.q:
Where does the comma belong?
“After the long drive through the mountains we finally stopped for food.”
comma_castle.why: An introductory element takes one comma at its end — where the introduction stops and the main sentence starts.

opts: The novel that won the prize is out of print.
The novel, that won the prize is out of print.
The novel that won the prize, is out of print.
The novel, that won the prize, is out of print.
comma_castle.why: A “that” clause is essential — it tells you which novel — so it takes no commas at all.

comma_castle.q: Which sentence contains an illegal comma?
opts: The tall man in the grey coat, waved.
The tall man in the grey coat waved.
The man, who wore grey, waved.
comma_castle.why: Never put a single comma between a subject and its verb. “The tall man … waved” has to stay joined.

comma_castle.q:
Choose the correct joining:
“The engine had failed ___ the crew kept working.”
comma_castle.why: Two complete sentences join with a comma AND a FANBOYS conjunction — both, never one alone.

opts: We left early because the road was flooded.
We left early, because the road was flooded.
We, left early because the road was flooded.
We left, early because the road was flooded.
comma_castle.why: A dependent clause that trails the main clause needs no comma. Move it to the front and it would.

comma_castle.q: Which sentence punctuates the pair of adjectives correctly?
opts: It was a cold, damp morning.
It was a cold damp, morning.
It was a, cold damp morning.
It was a cold, damp, morning.
comma_castle.why: Two adjectives that each modify the noun separately take a comma between them — but never between the last adjective and the noun.

equation_station.why: Divide by 2 first: x + 4 = 9. Distributing works too, but dividing is faster.
Move the 8 across (4x = 16), then divide by 4.
Combine like terms: (2 + 5)x. The exponent does not change.

equation_station.q: If x + y = 6 and x − y = 2, then x =
equation_station.why: Add the two equations and y cancels: 2x = 8.
Add 3x to both sides, then divide everything by 2 — including the 12.
Subtract 5, then divide by −2 — and dividing by a negative flips the inequality sign.

equation_station.q: A line has slope 3 and passes through (0, −4). Its equation is:
equation_station.why: Slope-intercept form is y = mx + b, and (0, −4) gives the intercept directly.

vocab_vault.q:
“Her approach was methodical: every trial logged, every variable controlled.”
As used here, methodical most nearly means:
vocab_vault.why: The colon explains the word: logged trials and controlled variables describe organisation. “Slow” is the trap — plausible about a person, unsupported by this sentence.

vocab_vault.q:
“The engineers proposed a novel solution to the bridge problem.”
Novel most nearly means:
vocab_vault.why: A solution cannot be fictional. Substitute each choice back into the sentence and only one survives.

vocab_vault.q:
“Asked about the delays, the director gave a candid response.”
Candid most nearly means:
vocab_vault.why: Candid is frank and unguarded — the opposite of rehearsed or evasive.

vocab_vault.q:
“The critic’s scathing review upset the author for weeks.”
Scathing most nearly means:
vocab_vault.why: It upset the author for weeks, so the review must have been severe.

vocab_vault.q:
“The soil here is poor, but the vines exploit it: their roots drive nine metres down to reach water no weed can find.”
As used here, exploit most nearly means:
vocab_vault.why: The everyday sense of “exploit” is negative, but the sentence admires the vines. Context beats habit.

vocab_vault.q:
“For thirty years the theory was orthodox; the students who questioned it were quietly not renewed.”
Orthodox most nearly means:
vocab_vault.why: The second clause shows the cost of disagreeing with it, which tells you it was the established view.

vocab_vault.q:
“She was frank about the risk, and the crew appreciated it.”
Frank most nearly means:
vocab_vault.why: The crew appreciated it, so the word must be positive — which rules out “severe”.

vocab_vault.q:
“The committee’s report was exhaustive: four hundred pages, six appendices, every objection answered.”
Exhaustive most nearly means:
vocab_vault.why: The colon lists evidence of completeness. “Tiring” borrows from “exhausting”, a different word.

vocab_vault.q:
“His account of the crossing is sober, and duller for it — no storms, no heroics, only distances and dates.”
Sober most nearly means:
vocab_vault.why: The dash defines it: no storms and no heroics. “Accurate” is tempting but the sentence never claims truth, only plainness.

vocab_vault.q:
“The fossil record here is spotty, so any story we tell about the period has to be held loosely.”
Spotty most nearly means:
vocab_vault.why: The consequence — holding the story loosely — points to gaps in the record rather than to poor workmanship.

apostrophe_alley.why: “its” = belonging to the team. “it’s” = “it is”. There is no such word as “its’”.

apostrophe_alley.q: Which is correct for a locker room shared by many players?
apostrophe_alley.why: A plural noun that already ends in s takes just an apostrophe after it.

apostrophe_alley.q:
Fill in:
“___ going to love ___ new coach.”
apostrophe_alley.why: “They’re” = they are; “their” shows possession; “there” is a place.

apostrophe_alley.q: Which sentence makes the plural without an apostrophe?
apostrophe_alley.why: Plain plural “dogs” takes no apostrophe; “their” shows possession.

apostrophe_alley.q: Which shows one boss owning an office?
apostrophe_alley.why: A singular noun takes ’s even when it already ends in s. The last choice would mean several bosses share it.

apostrophe_alley.q: Which sentence writes the decade correctly?
apostrophe_alley.why: A decade is a plain plural, not a possessive. No apostrophe.

apostrophe_alley.q:
Fill in:
“___ coat is on the chair?”
apostrophe_alley.why: “Whose” asks about possession. “Who’s” only ever means “who is” or “who has”.

apostrophe_alley.q: Ana and Ben jointly own one car. Which is correct?
apostrophe_alley.why: Joint ownership marks only the last name. Marking both would mean they own a car each.

apostrophe_alley.q: Which shows the possessive of an irregular plural?
apostrophe_alley.why: “Children” is already plural without an s, so it takes an ordinary ’s.

apostrophe_alley.q:
Fill in:
“___ sure that ___ notes are complete.”

opts: The storm knocked out the power.
Because the storm knocked out the power.
The storm, knocking out the power.
When the storm hit last night.
fragment_forest.why: It has a subject (storm), a real verb (knocked), and a complete thought.

fragment_forest.q:
Best fix:
“The runners stretched. Before the race began.”
fragment_forest.why: “Before the race began” is a fragment — attach it to the main clause.

fragment_forest.q:
Which fixes the run-on?
“I studied all night I still felt unready.”
fragment_forest.why: Two full sentences need a semicolon, a period, or a comma + FANBOYS.

fragment_forest.q: Which group of words is a fragment because a subordinator opens it?
fragment_forest.why: “Although” turns a complete thought into a dependent clause, which now needs a main clause to finish it.

fragment_forest.q:
Best fix:
“The team practicing all afternoon in the heat.”
opts: The team practiced all afternoon in the heat.
The team, practicing all afternoon in the heat.
Practicing all afternoon in the heat.
fragment_forest.why: “Practicing” on its own is not a verb a sentence can run on. It needs a real one: “practiced”.

fragment_forest.q:
Which fixes the run-on with a conjunction?
“The bell rang no one moved.”
fragment_forest.why: Comma + FANBOYS joins two complete sentences, and the comma goes before the conjunction, not after it.

fragment_forest.q: Which group of words is a fragment because a relative pronoun opens it?
opts: Which was the best part of the trip.
That was the best part of the trip.
The best part was the trip.
fragment_forest.why: A relative clause beginning “which” cannot stand alone — it modifies something in another sentence.

fragment_forest.q: Which sentence is missing a verb?
opts: The long queue outside the theatre in the rain.
The queue stretched outside the theatre.
fragment_forest.why: There is a subject and plenty of description, but nothing the subject actually does.

fragment_forest.q:
Best fix:
“She rewrote the essay, it was much stronger.”
fragment_forest.why: That is a comma splice. Adding a FANBOYS conjunction makes the join legal.

fragment_forest.q: A sentence needs a subject and a verb — though the subject may be understood. Which of these qualifies?
fragment_forest.why: A command has an understood subject (you) and a real verb. One word can be a whole sentence.

dash_dungeon.q:
Choose the correct punctuation:
“Her goal ___ a perfect score ___ drove every session.”
dash_dungeon.why: Dashes setting off extra info must come as a matched pair.

opts: She had one rule: never quit.
She had: one rule never quit.
She had one: rule never quit.
She had one rule; never quit:
dash_dungeon.why: A colon follows a complete sentence, then introduces the point.

opts: The bus was late; we missed the opening.
The bus was late, we missed the opening.
The bus was late we missed the opening.
The bus was late: we missed—
dash_dungeon.why: A semicolon joins two complete, related sentences.

dash_dungeon.q: Which sentence introduces the list correctly?
opts: I packed rope, a torch, and water.
I packed: rope, a torch, and water.
I packed — rope, a torch, and water.
I packed; rope, a torch, and water.
dash_dungeon.why: A colon needs a complete sentence in front of it. “I packed” is not one — it is still waiting for its object.

opts: Only one thing stopped her — fear.
Only one thing stopped her, — fear.
Only one thing stopped her — fear —.
Only one thing — stopped her fear.
dash_dungeon.why: A single dash is legal when the extra material runs to the end of the sentence; there it needs no partner.

dash_dungeon.q:
What is wrong with:
“The route — steep, icy, and long, was closed.”
opts: the pair is mismatched: a dash opens it and a comma closes it
a dash may never set off a list
dash_dungeon.why: Dashes and commas are both legal fences, but the two ends have to match each other.

dash_dungeon.q:
Choose the correct punctuation:
“The trail was flooded ___ however, we pressed on.”
dash_dungeon.why: “However” joining two sentences needs a semicolon before it; a comma there is a splice.

dash_dungeon.q: Which sentence punctuates the explanation correctly?
opts: The result was clear: the bridge would not hold.
The result was clear, the bridge would not hold.
The result was clear the bridge would not hold.
The result was clear — the bridge would not hold:
dash_dungeon.why: A colon is right when the second half delivers or explains the first. The comma version is a splice.

opts: We stopped — the engine was smoking — and waited.
We stopped — the engine was smoking and waited.
We stopped, the engine was smoking — and waited.
We stopped — the engine was smoking, — and waited.
dash_dungeon.why: An interruption mid-sentence takes a dash on both sides, and the sentence must still read correctly once the interruption is removed.

opts: We visited Lima, Peru; Quito, Ecuador; and Bogotá, Colombia.
We visited Lima, Peru, Quito, Ecuador, and Bogotá, Colombia.
We visited Lima; Peru, Quito; Ecuador, and Bogotá; Colombia.
We visited: Lima, Peru, Quito, Ecuador and Bogotá, Colombia.
dash_dungeon.why: When the items themselves contain commas, semicolons separate the items so the reader can see where each one ends.

verb_valley.q:
Choose the verb:
“The box of old photographs ___ in the attic.”
verb_valley.why: The subject is “box” (singular). Cross out “of old photographs” and the agreement is obvious.

verb_valley.q:
Keep the tense consistent:
“She opened the door and ___ inside.”
verb_valley.why: Past “opened” needs past “stepped”. Verbs joined by “and” share a tense.

verb_valley.q:
Choose the verb:
“Neither of the answers ___ correct.”
verb_valley.why: “Neither” is singular, however plural the phrase after it sounds.

verb_valley.q:
Choose the verb:
“The list of items ___ on the desk.”
verb_valley.why: The subject is “list” (singular); “of items” is just a prepositional phrase.

verb_valley.q:
Choose the verb:
“The committee ___ its decision on Friday.”
verb_valley.why: A collective noun acting as one body is singular — and “its” later in the sentence confirms it.

verb_valley.q:
Choose the verb:
“There ___ three reasons to be cautious.”
verb_valley.why: In a “there ___” sentence the real subject comes after the verb. Here it is “reasons”, which is plural.

verb_valley.q:
Choose the verb:
“By the time we arrived, the film ___ already started.”
verb_valley.why: The earlier of two past events takes the past perfect: it had started before we arrived.

verb_valley.q:
Choose the verb:
“The coach, along with two players, ___ the award.”
verb_valley.why: “Along with” does not make a compound subject. The subject is still “the coach”, singular.

verb_valley.q:
Choose the verb:
“The director and the producer ___ on the script.”
verb_valley.why: Two nouns joined by “and” make a genuine plural subject.

verb_valley.q:
Choose the verb:
“Either the manager or the assistants ___ the keys.”
verb_valley.why: With “either … or”, the verb matches whichever subject is nearer. “Assistants” is nearer, and plural.

transition_tower.q: “The plan was expensive. ___, it worked flawlessly.”
transition_tower.why: Expensive set against worked-well is a contrast, so the transition has to turn.

transition_tower.q: “He trained for months. ___, he was ready.”
transition_tower.why: Training leads to readiness — cause and effect, not contrast.

transition_tower.q:
Which is most concise?
“The results were clear ___ obvious to everyone.”
transition_tower.why: The ACT rewards concision, and stacked linkers are redundant by definition.

transition_tower.q: “It was raining hard. ___, the game continued.”
transition_tower.why: Rain would stop a game; the game continuing is the surprise, so the transition concedes.

transition_tower.q: “Several materials resist corrosion. ___, titanium survives years in seawater.”
transition_tower.why: The second sentence is one instance of the general claim in the first.

transition_tower.q: “The engine is quiet. ___, it uses half the fuel.”
transition_tower.why: Both facts point the same way, and the second adds to the first.

transition_tower.q:
Which is best?
“She checked the figures twice. ___ she submitted the report.”
transition_tower.why: These are two steps in sequence. Nothing is being contrasted or illustrated.

transition_tower.q: “The bridge closed for repairs. ___, traffic was rerouted through the valley.”
transition_tower.why: The rerouting is the result of the closure — a consequence, not a concession.

transition_tower.q: The paragraph already says the experiment failed, then explains why. The best transition before the explanation is:
transition_tower.why: An explanation follows the claim it explains. Three of these announce a turn that does not happen.

transition_tower.q:
Which choice is best?
“The soil was poor. However, moreover, the crop failed.”
transition_tower.why: Poor soil and a failed crop already follow one another. Two transitions contradict each other, and neither is needed.

fraction_falls.q: A shirt goes from $40 to $50. The percent increase is:
fraction_falls.why: change / original = 10/40 = 25%. The original is the denominator, always.

fraction_falls.q: A price rises 20%, then falls 20%. Against the start it is:
fraction_falls.why: 1.20 × 0.80 = 0.96. The second 20% is taken off a bigger number than the first was added to.

fraction_falls.q: Split 40 in the ratio 5 : 3. The larger part is:
fraction_falls.why: 8 parts in total, so each part is 5 — and the larger share is 5 of them.

fraction_falls.q: A value changes from 80 to 72. That is a:

fraction_falls.why: Dividing by a fraction means multiplying by its reciprocal: 3/4 × 3/2.
part / whole = 18/24 = 0.75. The number after “of” is the whole.

geometry_grotto.why: The radius is half the diameter, so r = 5 and area = πr² = 25π.

geometry_grotto.q: A triangle has base 8 and height 5. Its area is:
Two angles of a triangle are 90° and 40°. The third is:
A circle has radius 2. Its circumference is:
geometry_grotto.why: Circumference = 2πr. Area would be 4π too — read which one is asked.

geometry_grotto.q: A rectangle is 12 by 6. Its perimeter is:
geometry_grotto.why: Perimeter = 2(l + w) = 2(18). The 72 is the area.

A cylinder has radius 3 and height 10. Its volume is:
The interior angles of a regular hexagon each measure:
geometry_grotto.why: Interior angles sum to (n − 2)180° = 720°, shared equally among six.

geometry_grotto.q: Two similar triangles have sides in the ratio 2 : 3. Their areas are in the ratio:
geometry_grotto.why: Area scales with the square of the length ratio. 8 : 27 would be volume.

geometry_grotto.q: A square has area 49. Its perimeter is:
geometry_grotto.why: Each side is √49 = 7, and a square has four of them.

function_foundry.why: Work from the inside out: g(3) = 5, then f(5) = 25.

function_foundry.q: The graph of y = (x − 4)² is y = x² shifted:
function_foundry.why: A change inside the parentheses shifts horizontally, and it moves opposite the sign.

function_foundry.q: If f(x) = x² − 1, what is f(−3)?
function_foundry.why: (−3)² is 9, not −9. Square first, then subtract.

function_foundry.q: What is the domain of f(x) = 1/(x − 5)?
function_foundry.why: The denominator may never be zero, and it is zero exactly when x = 5.

function_foundry.q: If f(x) = 2x + 1, what is its inverse?
function_foundry.why: Swap x and y, then solve: x = 2y + 1 gives y = (x − 1)/2.

function_foundry.q: The graph of y = x² + 3 is y = x² shifted:
function_foundry.why: A constant added outside the squaring moves the whole curve vertically, in the direction of the sign.
A constant function ignores its input. Every output is 5.

function_foundry.q: For f(x) = x² − 4x, which x makes f(x) = 0?
function_foundry.why: Factor out x: x(x − 4) = 0, so either factor may be zero.

function_foundry.q: The range of f(x) = x² is:
function_foundry.why: A square is never negative, and zero is reachable at x = 0 — so the boundary is included.

trig_trench.why: The 5-12-13 triple: √(25 + 144) = 13. Adding the legs gives 17, which is the trap.
A half turn is π radians. A full turn is 2π.

trig_trench.q: Right triangle: opposite 8, adjacent 15, hypotenuse 17. tan θ =
trig_trench.why: tan = opposite / adjacent. The hypotenuse plays no part.

In a right triangle the two non-right angles must:
trig_trench.why: All three sum to 180°, and the right angle already uses 90° of it.

trig_trench.q: A 30-60-90 triangle has short leg 5. Its hypotenuse is:
trig_trench.why: In a 30-60-90 the hypotenuse is always twice the short leg. 5√3 is the long leg.
One of the three values worth memorising. cos 30° is the √3/2 one.

trig_trench.q: A ladder leans at 60° to the ground, reaching 12 m up a wall. Which finds its length L?
trig_trench.why: The 12 m is opposite the 60° angle and L is the hypotenuse, so it is a sine relationship.

trig_trench.q: An angle of 2π/3 radians is how many degrees?

probability_peaks.why: Independent events joined by AND multiply: ½ × ½.

probability_peaks.why: favourable / total = 3/5. The total is 5, not 3.

probability_peaks.q: P(at least one head in two flips) =
probability_peaks.why: “At least one” is easiest backwards: 1 − P(none) = 1 − ¼.

probability_peaks.why: One favourable outcome out of six equally likely ones.

probability_peaks.q: A fair six-sided die is rolled. P(an even number) =
probability_peaks.why: Three of the six faces are even.

probability_peaks.q: Two marbles are drawn without replacement from 4 red and 2 blue. P(both red) =
probability_peaks.why: The second draw sees a changed bag: (4/6) × (3/5) = 2/5.

probability_peaks.why: Independent choices multiply, they do not add.

main_idea_meadow.q:
“Cities were long treated as ecological deserts. Recent surveys have found otherwise: an inner-city churchyard in Berlin holds more bee species than the farmland around it, and abandoned rail sidings across Europe shelter plants now rare in the countryside. The reason is not that cities are kind, but that they are untidy — and untidiness, it turns out, is habitat.”
The main idea of the passage is that:
opts: cities support more wildlife than expected, because they are unmanaged
Berlin churchyards are unusually rich in bees
farmland has become hostile to insects
rail sidings should be protected by law
main_idea_meadow.why: The examples all serve one claim, stated in the last sentence. Two of the wrong choices are single details lifted out of the passage.

main_idea_meadow.q:
“The first mechanical clocks did not tell the time. They rang it. Housed in monastery towers, they existed to strike the hours of prayer, and their faces — when they had faces at all — were an afterthought. Only when clocks moved into markets and counting-houses did the dial become the point.”
The passage is primarily concerned with:
opts: how the purpose of early clocks differed from ours
the religious life of medieval monasteries
main_idea_meadow.why: Every sentence contrasts what clocks were for then with what they are for now. The monastery is setting, not subject.

main_idea_meadow.q:
“Translators used to be judged on fidelity to the words. The better test, I think, is fidelity to the effect. A joke that is rendered exactly and lands flat has been mistranslated, whatever the dictionary says.”
The author’s main point is that:
opts: a translation should reproduce a text’s effect rather than its wording
main_idea_meadow.why: The third sentence is an example supporting the claim in the second. The first sentence is the view being argued against.

main_idea_meadow.q:
“My grandmother kept her accounts in a hardback notebook, one line per day, in a hand that never varied. I have the notebooks still. They record no feeling of any kind — only flour, coal, thread, and the price of each. And yet you can see the year my grandfather fell ill in the widening gaps between entries.”
The passage is mainly about:
opts: how a plain record can reveal what it does not say
the cost of household goods in the past
main_idea_meadow.why: The turn comes at “And yet”. The notebooks matter because of what shows through them, not for their contents.

main_idea_meadow.q:
“Every few years someone announces that the essay is dying. The form has been declared dead on the arrival of the newspaper, the radio, the television and the internet, and has outlived each announcement. What actually happens is that the essay moves house.”
The main idea is that the essay:
opts: keeps surviving by adapting to new media
is genuinely in decline at last
is superior to radio and television
main_idea_meadow.why: The last sentence supplies the author’s own answer to the claim reported in the first.

main_idea_meadow.q:
“Coral bleaching is often described as a die-off, but a bleached reef is not yet a dead one. The coral has expelled the algae it lives with, and in cooler water it can take them back. Whether it does depends almost entirely on how long the heat lasts.”
The passage is primarily concerned with:
opts: correcting a common misunderstanding about bleaching
arguing that reefs are not endangered
describing methods of measuring sea temperature
main_idea_meadow.why: It opens by naming a wrong belief and spends the rest of its length qualifying it. It never claims reefs are safe.

main_idea_meadow.q:
“The standard history credits three engineers with the tunnel. The payroll ledgers name eleven hundred people. Most of them appear once, spelled differently each time, and then not again.”
The main idea is that:
opts: the accepted account leaves out most of the people who built the tunnel
the three engineers did not deserve credit
eleven hundred workers died during construction
main_idea_meadow.why: The contrast between three and eleven hundred carries the point. The passage never says the engineers deserved nothing.

main_idea_meadow.q:
“Birdsong is learned, not inherited, and a chick raised in silence sings a thin, disordered version of its species’ song. Raised among the wrong species, it learns the wrong song. The template is inherited; the performance is taught.”
The best statement of the main idea is:
opts: song depends on both inheritance and learning
birds cannot sing without hearing other birds
chicks raised in silence never sing
song is entirely a matter of upbringing
main_idea_meadow.why: The final sentence splits the credit between the two. The other three each overstate one half.

main_idea_meadow.q:
“A map is a claim about what matters. The road atlas in my car shows no rivers under fifty metres wide and no hill under a hundred metres high, which is to say it has decided, on my behalf, what a landscape is.”
The passage is mainly about:
opts: how maps encode the priorities of their makers
the measurement of rivers and hills
main_idea_meadow.why: The opening sentence states the claim and the rest of the passage is the single example that supports it.

main_idea_meadow.q:
“Sourdough is not a recipe but a relationship. The starter is a population of yeasts and bacteria that shifts with the flour you feed it, the water you use and the temperature of your kitchen; two bakers following identical instructions will not make the same loaf, and after a month they will not have the same starter either.”
The main idea is that sourdough baking:
opts: depends on living conditions that cannot be standardised
is more difficult than other baking
main_idea_meadow.why: The metaphor in the first sentence is cashed out by the second. Nothing here ranks sourdough against other baking.

detail_desert.q:
“The survey ran for six weeks in the spring of 1974. Of the two hundred nests examined, forty-one held eggs that never hatched; of those, the team attributed twenty-nine to cold and the rest to predation.”
According to the passage, how many unhatched clutches were attributed to predation?
detail_desert.why: 41 unhatched, 29 from cold, so “the rest” is 12. The passage makes you do one subtraction rather than handing you the number.

detail_desert.q:
“Ferns reproduce by spore, not by seed, and a single frond may release millions. Almost none survive. The spore must land on ground that is damp, shaded and already free of competitors — three conditions that rarely coincide.”
The passage states that a spore needs ground that is:
detail_desert.why: Go back and read the list. Two of the wrong choices change exactly one item, which is how detail traps are built.

detail_desert.q:
“Ada Lovelace’s notes on the Analytical Engine run to about three times the length of the paper she was translating. It is in the notes, not the paper, that she describes a machine operating on symbols rather than numbers.”
According to the passage, the description of a symbol-processing machine appears in:
detail_desert.why: The second sentence names the location explicitly, and sets it against the obvious wrong answer in the same breath.

detail_desert.q:
“The lighthouse was automated in 1982. The last keeper, Mairead Quinn, had served eleven years; her predecessor served thirty-four, and the one before him died in post after nine.”
How long did the keeper before Quinn’s predecessor serve?
detail_desert.why: Three keepers are named in reverse order. Reading the chain carefully is the whole task.

detail_desert.q:
“Roman concrete used volcanic ash from the Bay of Naples. Modern analysis shows that seawater reacts with this ash to grow a rare mineral inside the cracks, so that harbour walls two thousand years old are stronger now than when they were poured.”
According to the passage, the mineral forms as a result of:
opts: the weight of the harbour walls
detail_desert.why: The passage gives one cause. The other three are the kind of plausible mechanism a reader supplies from memory.

detail_desert.q:
“Between 1911 and 1913 the museum acquired eleven paintings, of which it had authenticated only four at the time of purchase. Three of the remaining seven were later shown to be copies.”
How many of the eleven paintings remained neither authenticated at purchase nor shown to be copies?
detail_desert.why: 11 − 4 authenticated = 7; 7 − 3 copies = 4. Detail questions on the ACT often hide one subtraction.

detail_desert.q:
“Monarch butterflies do not complete the migration in one lifetime. The generation that leaves Mexico in spring dies in Texas; it is the third or fourth generation that reaches Canada, and a single long-lived autumn generation that flies the whole way back.”
According to the passage, which generation makes the entire southward journey?
detail_desert.why: The last clause answers it. The trap is that several generations are named going north.

detail_desert.q:
“The glacier has retreated 2.4 kilometres since the first survey in 1894. Two-thirds of that loss has occurred since 1980.”
Approximately how far did the glacier retreat between 1894 and 1980?
detail_desert.why: Two-thirds came after 1980, so one-third — about 0.8 km — came before it.

detail_desert.q:
“Tea reached Britain through Portuguese and Dutch traders decades before the East India Company took an interest. Samuel Pepys records drinking it in 1660; the Company did not ship its first direct cargo until 1669.”
According to the passage, Pepys drank tea:
opts: nine years before the Company’s first direct cargo
in the same year as the Company’s first cargo
after the Company began direct trade
detail_desert.why: 1669 − 1660 = 9. The last choice contradicts the passage outright.

detail_desert.q:
“The report lists three causes of the failure and ranks them. Poor drainage is first; the sequence of the concrete pours is second; the choice of aggregate, which the press seized on, is third and least significant.”
The passage indicates that the aggregate was:
opts: the least significant of the three causes
detail_desert.why: The passage ranks it explicitly, and flags that the press got the emphasis wrong.

inference_icefield.q:
“She set down the letter and stared out of the window for a long time.”
It can reasonably be inferred that:
inference_icefield.why: Take the smallest supported step. The other three invent facts the sentence does not carry.

inference_icefield.q:
“The café had been there forty years. The new sign was in a typeface the owner’s daughter had chosen, and the prices had gone up by a third, and the regulars still came, but earlier, and they did not stay.”
It can be inferred that the regulars:
opts: could no longer afford the café
had moved out of the area
inference_icefield.why: They still come, so they can afford it and have not moved. The change in how they come is the evidence.

inference_icefield.q:
“Every reference in the bibliography predates 1961, though the book was published in 1974.”
This most strongly suggests that:
opts: the author did not engage with recent work
the bibliography is incomplete by accident
inference_icefield.why: The gap is the point. Saying the book was written in 1961 goes further than the evidence allows.

inference_icefield.q:
“He wrote to his brother twice a week for eleven years. The letters from the last year are shorter, and in three of them he asks a question he had asked the month before.”
It can reasonably be inferred that in the last year he was:
opts: losing his memory or his grip on the correspondence
no longer interested in his brother’s replies
inference_icefield.why: Repeating a question he recently asked is the specific evidence. Anger and disinterest would not produce that detail.

inference_icefield.q:
“The recipe calls for the dough to rest overnight. My mother never let it. She said the waiting was for people with cold kitchens.”
It can be inferred that the mother believed:
opts: her kitchen was warm enough to make the rest unnecessary
the recipe was wrong in every respect
she was a better cook than the recipe’s author
inference_icefield.why: Her reason names the condition the rest is for, and implies her kitchen does not meet it.

inference_icefield.q:
“The company’s annual report devotes eleven pages to its environmental programme and one paragraph to the closure of its two largest plants.”
The proportions most strongly suggest that the report is:
opts: shaped more by presentation than by significance
a complete account of the year
inference_icefield.why: The mismatch between space and importance is the inference. Nothing supports a legal claim.

inference_icefield.q:
“When the interviewer asked about the second trial, the researcher said the data were still being cleaned, and moved on to the third.”
It can reasonably be inferred that the researcher:
opts: preferred not to discuss the second trial
had not conducted a second trial
inference_icefield.why: Answering and immediately changing subject is the evidence. Whether the data really were unclean is beside the point.

inference_icefield.q:
“The island’s only bookshop orders four copies of each new novel. It has never ordered a fifth.”
It can be inferred that:
opts: demand on the island is small and predictable
the island has few readers of any kind
four is the publisher’s minimum order
inference_icefield.why: Consistency across many titles implies the owner knows the market. “Few readers of any kind” overreaches — this is one shop and one genre.

inference_icefield.q:
“He kept the receipts for everything he bought that year, and the following January he wrote out a list of what he wished he had not.”
It can be inferred that he:
opts: was reviewing his own spending habits
had been asked to account for the money
inference_icefield.why: The list is made for himself, after the fact. Returning goods and being audited both require someone else in the picture.

inference_icefield.q:
“The tide table is printed on the wall of the harbour office, and beside it, in a different hand, someone has written: “Add twenty minutes in the channel.””
The added note most strongly suggests that:
opts: the printed table is not quite accurate for local conditions
the table is out of date by twenty minutes
the harbour office is poorly run
inference_icefield.why: A local correction implies a local discrepancy. That is a narrower claim than the table being wrong everywhere.

viewpoint_vista.q:
Writer A: Rewilding works because it stops managing. Left alone, the land finds an arrangement more robust than any we design.
Writer B: There is no “alone” left. The soils are altered, the herbivores are gone, and doing nothing simply hands the ground to whatever arrived last.
Both writers would agree that:
opts: human activity has already changed the land
viewpoint_vista.why: A implies past management; B states past alteration outright. The other three are exactly what they disagree about.

viewpoint_vista.q:
Writer A: Standardised tests are the only instrument that treats every applicant identically.
Writer B: Identical treatment is not fair treatment when preparation is purchasable.
Their disagreement is best described as:
opts: whether applicants differ from one another
viewpoint_vista.why: B does not dispute A’s fact; she disputes what it is worth. Locating the hinge is the whole skill.

viewpoint_vista.q:
Writer A: The city should widen the ring road; congestion costs the region millions in lost hours.
Writer B: Every widening in this city’s history has filled within four years.
Writer B responds to Writer A by:
opts: citing evidence that the proposed remedy does not last
questioning the accuracy of the cost figures
viewpoint_vista.why: B never argues with the cost of congestion — only with whether widening fixes it.

viewpoint_vista.q:
Writer A: Museums should return contested objects without waiting for perfect provenance.
Writer B: Return the wrong object to the wrong claimant and you have committed a second theft.
Writer B’s main concern is:
opts: the risk of acting on incomplete information
whether the objects were stolen at all
viewpoint_vista.why: B accepts that theft occurred — that is what “a second theft” concedes — and worries only about error.

viewpoint_vista.q:
Writer A: Remote work has made teams more productive and people happier.
Writer B: It has made experienced people more productive and new hires invisible.
Writer B’s position is best described as:
viewpoint_vista.why: B grants part of A’s claim and restricts it to a group. That is qualification, not contradiction.

viewpoint_vista.q:
Writer A: Any language with fewer than a thousand speakers will be gone within two generations.
Writer B: Hebrew had no native speakers at all and now has nine million.
Writer B’s use of Hebrew serves to:
opts: offer a counterexample to a general rule
change the subject to ancient languages
question the count of a thousand speakers
viewpoint_vista.why: One case that breaks the rule is the classic way to answer a universal claim.

viewpoint_vista.q:
Writer A: The painting is certainly by the master; the underdrawing matches his workshop practice.
Writer B: The underdrawing matches the practice of his workshop — which employed thirty people.
Writer B’s reply works by:
opts: showing the evidence supports a weaker conclusion
viewpoint_vista.why: B accepts the evidence exactly as given and shows it cannot carry the weight A puts on it.

viewpoint_vista.q:
Writer A: Nuclear power is the only low-carbon source that runs regardless of weather.
Writer B: It is also the only one that takes fifteen years to build.
The two writers differ mainly in:
opts: which drawback or advantage they treat as decisive
viewpoint_vista.why: Neither contradicts the other’s fact. They disagree about which fact should settle the question.

viewpoint_vista.q:
Writer A: Children should learn to write by hand before they type; the motor memory aids recognition.
Writer B: The studies showing that effect all predate touchscreens.
Writer B objects on the grounds that:
opts: the evidence may not apply to current conditions
viewpoint_vista.why: B raises the age of the evidence, not its quality or its conclusion.

viewpoint_vista.q:
Writer A: Subtitles let a film keep its own language.
Writer B: Subtitles let a film keep its own language while the audience looks at the bottom of the frame instead of the actor’s face.
Writer B’s sentence is best described as:
opts: conceding Writer A’s point and naming its cost
restating Writer A’s point in other words
viewpoint_vista.why: B repeats A’s clause word for word and then adds to it. The repetition is the concession.

graph_gorge.q: A graph shows three labelled curves and a legend. To answer a question about one of them, you should:
opts: follow the single curve the legend names
use the curve nearest the y-axis
graph_gorge.why: Identify the curve before reading any value. Most graph errors happen before the reading does.

graph_gorge.q: Where two curves on the same axes intersect, the two quantities are:
graph_gorge.why: An intersection is the one place the two y-values agree.

graph_gorge.q: A curve rises steeply, levels off, and stays flat. The flat portion shows that the quantity:
graph_gorge.why: A flat line means no change, not no quantity. Height and slope are different readings.

graph_gorge.q: On a graph of distance against time, a straight line means the speed is:
graph_gorge.why: Slope is speed here, and a straight line has one slope throughout.

graph_gorge.q: A scatterplot shows points scattered with no pattern from lower-left to upper-right or otherwise. This indicates:
opts: little or no relationship between the variables
graph_gorge.why: Absence of a trend is a finding. It is not, by itself, evidence that anything went wrong.

graph_gorge.q: A graph’s y-axis runs from 98 to 102. A curve that looks dramatic on this axis:
opts: may represent a very small real change
must represent a large real change
graph_gorge.why: Always read the axis range before judging a shape. A truncated axis magnifies everything.

graph_gorge.q: Two curves both rise, but curve P is always above curve Q. This shows that:
opts: P is greater than Q at every x shown
graph_gorge.why: Being above is about value; rising faster is about slope. Only the first is visible here.

graph_gorge.q: A quantity is plotted on a logarithmic y-axis. Equal vertical distances on that axis represent:
graph_gorge.why: On a log scale a fixed step means “times ten”, not “plus ten”.

graph_gorge.q: A curve peaks at x = 4 and falls on either side. The value of x that gives the maximum y is:
graph_gorge.why: Read the x-coordinate of the highest point, not the highest x on the axis.

graph_gorge.q: Extending a graph’s trend beyond the plotted data to predict a value is:
opts: extrapolation, and less reliable than reading within the data
the only way to use a graph
graph_gorge.why: Outside the measured range you are assuming the pattern continues, which the data never showed.

experiment_expanse.q: The variable the researchers deliberately change is the:
experiment_expanse.why: Independent = what is changed on purpose. Dependent = what you then measure.

experiment_expanse.q: The purpose of a control group is to:
opts: give a baseline with no treatment
experiment_expanse.why: Without a baseline there is nothing for the treated group to be different from.

experiment_expanse.q: If two variables change between trials, you:
opts: cannot tell which one caused the result
experiment_expanse.why: Changing one thing at a time is what makes a cause attributable.

experiment_expanse.q:
Students measured plant growth under three light colours, using the same soil, pot size and watering schedule throughout.
Soil, pot size and watering schedule are:
experiment_expanse.why: They are deliberately held constant so that light colour is the only thing that differs.

experiment_expanse.q:
A trial is repeated five times and the results averaged.
The main reason for repeating is to:
opts: reduce the effect of random variation
experiment_expanse.why: Repetition addresses noise. It cannot fix a design that measures the wrong thing.

experiment_expanse.q:
Experiment 1 heated the sample in air. Experiment 2 repeated it in nitrogen.
The purpose of Experiment 2 was most likely to test whether:
opts: oxygen was involved in the result
experiment_expanse.why: Swapping air for nitrogen removes oxygen and holds nearly everything else. The changed variable names the question.

experiment_expanse.q: A study finds that towns with more libraries have lower unemployment. The strongest objection is that:
opts: a third factor, such as town wealth, may explain both
experiment_expanse.why: Correlation invites a confounder. Naming a plausible one is the standard move.

experiment_expanse.q:
The thermometer used in all trials read 2 °C high.
This is best described as:
opts: a systematic error affecting every trial the same way
a reason to discard the experiment
experiment_expanse.why: A constant offset shifts every reading equally, so comparisons between trials survive it.

experiment_expanse.q:
Group A received the drug; Group B received an identical-looking pill with no active ingredient.
Group B is:
experiment_expanse.why: Matching everything except the active ingredient is what makes the comparison clean.

experiment_expanse.q: A result is reported from a single trial on one sample. The most reasonable response is to:
opts: treat it as preliminary until it is repeated
assume the researcher made an error
experiment_expanse.why: One trial is a start, not a conclusion — and doubting a result is not the same as disproving it.

conflict_canyon.q:
Scientist 1: The crater formed by meteorite impact; the quartz at the rim is shocked.
Scientist 2: It is volcanic. Shocked quartz also forms in explosive eruptions.
The two scientists disagree about:
conflict_canyon.why: They agree the quartz is there. They disagree about what it proves — which is where the questions will live.

conflict_canyon.q:
Scientist 1: The decline is caused by the new pesticide.
Scientist 2: The decline began four years before the pesticide was licensed.
Scientist 2’s point works by:
opts: showing the proposed cause came after the effect
conflict_canyon.why: A cause cannot follow its effect. That is the cleanest way to break a causal claim.

conflict_canyon.q:
Scientist 1: Birds navigate by the stars.
Scientist 2: They navigate by the earth’s magnetic field.
Which finding would support Scientist 2 over Scientist 1?
opts: Birds in a windowless room still orient correctly until a magnet is switched on
Birds released under cloud become disoriented
Young birds navigate less accurately than adults
conflict_canyon.why: It removes the stars and manipulates the magnetic field — testing exactly the difference between the two views.

conflict_canyon.q:
Scientist 1: The mass extinction was rapid, over a few thousand years.
Scientist 2: It took at least half a million years.
Both would most likely agree that:
opts: the timescale can be measured precisely
conflict_canyon.why: The shared ground is whatever neither disputes. They differ only on duration.

conflict_canyon.q:
Student 1: The metal expanded because it was heated.
Student 2: It expanded because it absorbed moisture.
Which result would weaken Student 2?
opts: The same expansion occurs in a sealed dry chamber
The metal expands more on humid days
conflict_canyon.why: Removing moisture entirely and still seeing the effect leaves Student 2 with nothing to explain it.

conflict_canyon.q:
Scientist 1: The lake’s algae bloom is driven by farm runoff.
Scientist 2: It is driven by warmer water.
New evidence that blooms occur in cold years after heavy fertiliser use would:
conflict_canyon.why: Cold years remove Scientist 2’s proposed driver while the blooms continue.

conflict_canyon.q:
Scientist 1: Dinosaurs were warm-blooded; their bone growth rings resemble those of mammals.
Scientist 2: Some modern reptiles kept warm by their environment show the same rings.
Scientist 2 is arguing that Scientist 1’s evidence is:
opts: consistent with more than one explanation
conflict_canyon.why: The evidence stands; what is challenged is its uniqueness as a signal.

conflict_canyon.q:
Scientist 1: Language ability is mostly innate.
Scientist 2: It is mostly learned from exposure.
A finding that children exposed to almost no speech still form grammatical rules would:
conflict_canyon.why: Rules appearing without input is precisely what an innate account predicts and a learning account does not.

conflict_canyon.q:
Scientist 1: The sediment layer was laid down by a flood.
Scientist 2: It was laid down by wind.
Which observation best distinguishes the two?
opts: Whether the grains are rounded and well sorted by size
conflict_canyon.why: Wind sorts grains far more strictly than water does, so grain sorting is the discriminating observation.

conflict_canyon.q: When a conflicting-viewpoints passage gives two theories, a question asking what both scientists accept is answered by:
opts: the facts neither of them disputes
the first sentence of each theory
conflict_canyon.why: Shared ground sits in what both take for granted, not in either conclusion.

outside_outpost.why: Below 7 is acidic, above 7 is basic, 7 is neutral.

outside_outpost.q: Photosynthesis takes in carbon dioxide and light and releases:
outside_outpost.why: Plants release O₂ as a by-product.

outside_outpost.q: Pure water at sea level boils at:
outside_outpost.why: 100 °C — the 212 is the same temperature in Fahrenheit, which is the trap.

outside_outpost.q: In an atom, the particle with no charge is the:
outside_outpost.why: Protons are positive, electrons negative, neutrons neutral.

outside_outpost.q: Which of these is a chemical change rather than a physical one?
outside_outpost.why: A chemical change produces a new substance. The other three can be reversed without one.

outside_outpost.q: DNA is copied during which process?
outside_outpost.why: Replication copies DNA; translation builds protein from RNA.

outside_outpost.q: An object in motion stays in motion unless acted on by an external force. This is:
opts: the law of conservation of mass
outside_outpost.why: The first law is the law of inertia.

outside_outpost.q: The density of pure water is closest to:
outside_outpost.why: 1 gram per millilitre — worth knowing, because Science passages assume it without saying so.

outside_outpost.q: In a food chain, organisms that break down dead material are:
outside_outpost.why: Producers make their own food; decomposers return nutrients from dead matter.

outside_outpost.q: A question can be answered entirely from the figure provided. You should:
opts: add outside facts to the figure
outside_outpost.why: Outside knowledge is only needed when the passage supplies none. When the data answer it, the data win.

exponent_expanse.why: Multiplying powers of the same base adds the exponents: 3 + 4.
A power of a power multiplies the exponents: 2 × 3.
A negative exponent means reciprocal, not a negative number: 1/2².
Dividing powers of the same base subtracts the exponents.
Any non-zero base raised to the zero power is 1.
A square root is the ½ power, so the exponent halves: 6 × ½.
The outside exponent hits every factor inside, the 2 included: 2⁴ = 16.
Pull out the largest perfect square: 50 = 25 × 2.
The denominator is the root and the numerator is the power: (∛8)² = 2².
Add the exponents: 5 + (−5) = 0, and anything to the zero power is 1.

quadratic_quarry.why: Find two numbers that multiply to 12 and add to 7.
Zero-product rule: set each factor to zero. The signs flip.

quadratic_quarry.q: How many real solutions does x² = 16 have?
quadratic_quarry.why: Both 4 and −4 square to 16. Taking only the positive root loses one.
A difference of two squares always factors into a sum times a difference.
Factors to (x − 2)(x + 4) = 0. Check by expanding if the signs feel slippery.
In vertex form y = (x − h)² + k the vertex is (h, k), and h takes the opposite sign to the one written.

quadratic_quarry.q: In the quadratic formula, the discriminant is:
quadratic_quarry.why: It is the part under the root, and its sign tells you how many real solutions there are.
A negative under a square root leaves the real number line.
Always take out the greatest common factor first — here 2x.
A negative leading coefficient opens the curve downward; the +4 lifts the vertex.

statistics_summit.why: Sum is 30, and there are five values.
Sort first — 1, 2, 4, 7, 9 — then take the middle. Skipping the sort is the usual mistake.
5 appears three times, more than anything else.
With an even count there is no single middle, so average the two middle values.

statistics_summit.q: Adding the value 100 to the set 2, 3, 4 changes the mean and the median:
opts: mean a lot, median a little
median a lot, mean a little
statistics_summit.why: An outlier drags the mean toward itself but only nudges the median one position.

statistics_summit.q: A set of 5 numbers has mean 8. Their sum is:
statistics_summit.why: Mean × count = sum. Reading the mean formula backwards is a standard ACT move.

statistics_summit.q: Four tests average 82. What is needed on a fifth to average 84 over all five?
statistics_summit.why: Five tests at 84 need 420 points; four at 82 have given 328.

statistics_summit.q: Which is unaffected by one extreme outlier?
statistics_summit.why: The median depends only on position, not on how far out a value sits.

statistics_summit.q: A data set is 6, 6, 6, 6. Its standard deviation is:
statistics_summit.why: Nothing varies from the mean, so the spread is zero.

coordinate_cove.why: Average the x values and average the y values.

coordinate_cove.q: A line falling as you move right has a slope that is:
coordinate_cove.why: Downhill left-to-right means rise is negative while run is positive.

coordinate_cove.q: A vertical line has a slope that is:
coordinate_cove.why: The run is zero, and division by zero is undefined. A horizontal line is the one with slope zero.

coordinate_cove.q: Which line is parallel to y = 2x + 1?
coordinate_cove.why: Parallel lines share a slope; only the intercept may differ.

coordinate_cove.q: Which line is perpendicular to y = 2x + 1?
coordinate_cove.why: Perpendicular slopes are negative reciprocals: the opposite sign and the flipped fraction.

coordinate_cove.q: The point (−3, 5) lies in which quadrant?
coordinate_cove.why: Negative x with positive y is the upper-left quadrant.

coordinate_cove.q: Where does y = 3x − 6 cross the x-axis?
coordinate_cove.why: The x-axis is where y = 0. Setting y = 0 gives x = 2; (0, −6) is the y-intercept.

coordinate_cove.q: The circle (x − 1)² + (y + 2)² = 9 has centre and radius:
coordinate_cove.why: The centre takes the opposite signs to those written, and the right-hand side is r², not r.

coordinate_cove.q: Translating (4, −1) three units left and two units up gives:
coordinate_cove.why: Left subtracts from x; up adds to y.

units_uplands.why: Kilo means a thousand, so multiply.
Convert everything to one unit first: 1000 mm, 500 mm, 900 mm, 500 mm.

units_uplands.q: The same quantity expressed in a larger unit gives a number that is:
units_uplands.why: Bigger unit, fewer of them. It is the one check that catches a flipped conversion.
A thousand millilitres make a litre, so divide.

units_uplands.q: A rate given in grams per second is converted to grams per minute by:
units_uplands.why: More seconds in the window means more grams, so the number goes up.
Three dimensions multiplied gives a cubic unit. cm² is area.

units_uplands.q: A table lists concentration in µg/L and a question asks for mg/L. 4000 µg/L equals:
units_uplands.why: A milligram is a thousand micrograms, so divide by 1000.

units_uplands.q: Two data columns are headed “Mass (kg)” and “Mass (g)”. Comparing the numbers directly would:
opts: be meaningless until one column is converted
be valid because both are masses
units_uplands.why: Reading the unit in the column heading is the first thing to do, and the most commonly skipped.

units_uplands.q: A speed of 72 km/h in metres per second is:
units_uplands.why: 72 km is 72 000 m and an hour is 3600 s, so 72 000 ÷ 3600 = 20.

units_uplands.q: Temperature is recorded in kelvin. A reading of 273 K is approximately:
units_uplands.why: Kelvin and Celsius are offset by 273, so 273 K is water’s freezing point.

rates_ridge.q: A car travels 150 km in 3 hours. Its average speed is:
rates_ridge.why: Rate = amount ÷ time. Dividing, not multiplying, is the whole of it.

rates_ridge.q: A tap fills 12 litres in 4 minutes. How long to fill 30 litres at the same rate?
A reaction produces 6 g of gas in 30 seconds. Its rate is:
rates_ridge.why: 6 ÷ 30 = 0.2. If the answer looks large, check which number you divided by.

rates_ridge.q: Two pumps each move 8 L/min. Working together they move:
A population doubles every 3 years. After 9 years it has multiplied by:
rates_ridge.why: Three doublings: 2 × 2 × 2. Doubling periods multiply, they do not add.

rates_ridge.q: A runner covers the first 5 km at 10 km/h and the next 5 km at 5 km/h. Her average speed is:
rates_ridge.why: She spends twice as long on the slow half, so the slow speed carries more weight than the fast one.

rates_ridge.q: A tank loses 2 % of its contents each hour. After two hours it holds:
opts: slightly more than 96 % of the original
rates_ridge.why: The second 2 % is taken from a smaller amount, so the loss is slightly under 4 % in total.

rates_ridge.q: A printer prints 18 pages per minute. In 40 seconds it prints about:
rates_ridge.why: 40 seconds is two-thirds of a minute, so two-thirds of 18.

rates_ridge.q: Fuel use is 7 litres per 100 km. A 250 km journey uses about:
If a rate is constant, a graph of total amount against time is:
rates_ridge.why: Constant rate means constant slope. A flattening curve would mean a falling rate.
