pronoun_pass.q: “The coach gave the trophy to Sam and ___.”
pronoun_pass.why: It is the object of “to”. Drop “Sam and” and your ear does the rest.

pronoun_pass.q: “Each of the players ___ responsible for ___ gear.”
pronoun_pass.why: “Each” is singular, so both the verb and the pronoun that follow it are singular.

pronoun_pass.q: “The student ___ won the prize is here.”
pronoun_pass.why: It is the subject of “won”, and “who” is the subject form. “Which” never refers to a person.

pronoun_pass.q: “The scientist ___ the committee praised has published again.”
pronoun_pass.why: Here the committee did the praising, so the pronoun is the object — “whom”.

pronoun_pass.q: Which sentence has a clear pronoun reference?
opts: When Maya met Priya, Maya was nervous.
When Maya met Priya, she was nervous.
Maya met Priya, and she was nervous.
She was nervous when Maya met Priya.
pronoun_pass.why: Three of these leave “she” pointing at either woman. Repeating the name is clumsy but correct, and the ACT prefers correct.
A company is one thing. Keep it singular all the way through the sentence.
The sentence is short for “faster than I run”, so the subject form is right.

opts: The manager and I reviewed the budget.
The manager and myself reviewed the budget.
The manager and me reviewed the budget.
Myself and the manager reviewed the budget.
pronoun_pass.why: “Myself” is only for reflecting back on a subject already named. Here the pronoun is part of the subject.

pronoun_pass.q:
What is wrong with:
“The road was flooded and the bridge was out, which delayed us.”
opts: “which” has no single noun to refer to
pronoun_pass.why: A pronoun has to point at a noun, not at a whole situation. “A delay resulted” fixes it.

pronoun_pass.q: “Every one of the applicants submitted ___ portfolio.”
pronoun_pass.why: “Every one” is singular, so “their” clashes. Rewriting with an article sidesteps the clumsy “his or her”.

modifier_marsh.q:
Fix the dangler:
“Walking home, the rain started.”
opts: Walking home, I felt the rain start.
Walking home, the rain fell hard.
modifier_marsh.why: The subject right after the comma has to be the one doing the walking.

modifier_marsh.q:
Which means she finished nearly all of it?
“She ate ___ the pizza.”
modifier_marsh.why: “Almost” has to sit next to the word it limits — here, “all”.

opts: Tired from practice, Jordan went to bed.
Tired from practice, bed sounded great.
Tired from practice, the game ended.
Tired from practice, it got late.
modifier_marsh.why: Jordan is the one who is tired. A bed, a game and “it” cannot be.

modifier_marsh.q:
Where should “only” go?
“She ___ ate ___ the salad ___.” (she ate nothing else)
modifier_marsh.why: “Only” modifies whatever follows it. Put it before “the salad” and the salad is the sole thing eaten.

modifier_marsh.q: Which sentence gives the opening phrase something it can sensibly describe?
opts: Covered in dust, the hikers reached the hut.
Covered in dust, the hut appeared.
Covered in dust, it was a long walk.
The hut appeared covered in dust, exhausted.
modifier_marsh.why: The hikers are the ones covered in dust, so they must be the subject that follows.

modifier_marsh.q:
What is wrong with:
“We saw a deer driving through the park.”
opts: it reads as though the deer was driving
modifier_marsh.why: A participial phrase attaches to the nearest noun. Move it: “Driving through the park, we saw a deer.”

opts: She nearly walked the whole route.
She walked nearly the whole route.
Nearly she walked the whole route.
She walked the whole nearly route.
modifier_marsh.why: Placing “nearly” before “walked” says she almost did not walk at all. Before “the whole route” it says she covered most of it.

modifier_marsh.q: Which sentence avoids a dangling participle?
opts: Hoping for a better view, we climbed the ridge.
Hoping for a better view, the ridge was climbed.
Hoping for a better view, the view improved.
The ridge, hoping for a better view, was climbed.
modifier_marsh.why: A passive main clause is the classic dangler trap — the ridge cannot hope for anything.

modifier_marsh.q:
Fix the misplaced phrase:
“The letter was mailed by the lawyer in a blue envelope.”
opts: The lawyer mailed the letter in a blue envelope.
In a blue envelope the lawyer was mailed the letter.
The letter in a blue envelope was mailed by the lawyer in it.
modifier_marsh.why: As written, the lawyer is in the envelope. Move the phrase next to “letter”.

opts: After studying all week, she felt ready.
After studying all week, the exam felt easier.
After studying all week, it went well.
After studying all week, the results arrived.
modifier_marsh.why: She is the one who studied. Exams, results and “it” cannot study.

opts: She likes reading, writing, and drawing.
She likes reading, to write, and drawing.
She likes to read, writing, and draws.
parallel_pier.why: All three items are -ing forms. A list has to keep one shape throughout.
The first two items are nouns, so the third has to be a noun too.
Three adjectives describing the report. The other choices change grammatical shape mid-list.

parallel_pier.q:
Which is parallel?
“He came not only to watch but also ___.”
parallel_pier.why: “Not only … but also” has to bracket two identical structures. “To watch” demands “to compete”.

parallel_pier.q: “She would rather train early than ___ late.”
parallel_pier.why: “Rather … than” joins two bare verbs. “Train” demands “finish”.

parallel_pier.q: Which sentence keeps the three infinitives parallel?
opts: The course teaches students to plan, to draft, and to revise.
The course teaches students to plan, drafting, and to revise.
The course teaches students planning, to draft, and revision.
The course teaches students to plan, draft, and revising.
parallel_pier.why: Repeating “to” before each verb is one valid pattern; dropping it before all of them is another. Mixing the two is not.

parallel_pier.q: “The candidate promised both lower taxes and ___.”
parallel_pier.why: “Both … and” must bracket matching structures. A noun phrase demands a noun phrase.

parallel_pier.q: Which sentence keeps the three -ing forms parallel?
opts: We spent the day hiking, swimming, and resting.
We spent the day hiking, to swim, and rested.
We spent the day on a hike, swimming, and rested.
We spent the day hiking, swam, and resting.
parallel_pier.why: Three -ing forms in a row. The others swap form partway through.
The comparison is between two methods, so the possessive “his” — short for “his method” — is what balances it.

structure_span.q:
“For two centuries the disease was thought to travel in bad air. Then, in 1854, a physician mapped the deaths around a single water pump. The map did not persuade everyone at once, but the argument had changed shape: it was now about water, and it has stayed there.”
The passage is organised as:
opts: a long-held belief, a turning point, and its consequence
a claim followed by three supporting examples
a comparison of two competing cities
structure_span.why: Watch the time markers: “For two centuries”, “Then, in 1854”, “has stayed there”. They are the skeleton.

structure_span.q:
“Consider the cost first. Then consider what the cost buys. Then consider what is lost when the thing is not bought at all, which is the calculation nobody makes.”
The paragraph is structured as:
opts: a sequence of three framings, ending with the author’s own
a list of objections and replies
a general rule and its exceptions
structure_span.why: Three parallel imperatives, and the last one carries the relative clause that gives the author away.

structure_span.q:
“The bird is small, brown and unremarkable. Its song is small, brown and unremarkable. And yet it can navigate from Finland to Mozambique using, we now believe, a protein in its eye that responds to the earth’s magnetic field.”
The passage moves from:
structure_span.why: The pivot is “And yet”. Everything before it is deliberately flat so the turn can land.

structure_span.q:
“There are three objections. The first — that it is expensive — is true and unimportant. The second, that it is unpopular, is true and temporary. The third is that it will not work, and that one deserves a serious answer.”
The structure of this paragraph is best described as:
opts: an enumeration in which the items are ranked by seriousness
structure_span.why: It numbers three objections and dismisses the first two in a clause each to clear room for the third.

structure_span.q:
“Begin with a lemon. Its skin is a store of oil; its flesh is a store of acid; the two are used for opposite purposes and are almost never used together. Most of what follows in this book is an argument with that “almost”.”
The final sentence functions to:
opts: state the book’s subject by turning on a word in the previous sentence
structure_span.why: The quotation marks around “almost” do the work — the author has planted the word in order to pick it up.

structure_span.q:
“The engine failed at 04:10. The backup engaged at 04:11 and failed at 04:26. The crew had, by their own later account, believed until 04:31 that the backup was running.”
The paragraph is organised by:
opts: time, with the last sentence revealing a gap in what was known
cause and effect, with the cause stated last
a general rule and a specific case
structure_span.why: Three timestamps in order, and the fourth lands outside the sequence to show what the crew did not know.

structure_span.q:
“What is a weed? A plant in the wrong place. What is the wrong place? Wherever someone has other plans. The category, in other words, is not botanical at all.”
The passage proceeds by:
opts: a chain of questions and answers ending in a conclusion
a narrative of how weeds spread
a contrast between two kinds of plant
structure_span.why: Two question-and-answer pairs, then “in other words” signals the conclusion drawn from both.

structure_span.q:
“Everyone knows the story: an apple, a head, a law. It is almost certainly embroidered, and the embroidering was probably his own. But the story has done a job no equation could, which is to give the law a place to live in people who will never read it.”
The passage is structured as:
opts: a familiar claim, a doubt about it, and a defence of it on other grounds
a claim supported by three examples
a chronological account of a discovery
structure_span.why: Note “It is almost certainly” and then “But”. The author concedes the story is false and then argues it is useful anyway.

structure_span.q:
“The first paragraph of this report tells you what was found. The second tells you how. The third tells you what it cost, and it is the third that will be read.”
The final clause serves mainly to:
opts: comment wryly on the reader’s priorities
structure_span.why: Having laid out a neutral structure, the author adds a judgement about which part matters to people.

structure_span.q:
“Salt was money, then salt was cheap. The change took about eighty years and almost no one recorded it happening, because nothing that becomes ordinary is written down while it is becoming so.”
The second sentence relates to the first by:
opts: explaining why the change left little trace
giving an example of the change
restating the first sentence more precisely
structure_span.why: The first states the change; the second explains the absence of a record of it, with a general principle attached.

tone_tundra.q:
“The committee’s solution, arrived at after fourteen months, was to form a second committee.”
The tone of this sentence is best described as:
tone_tundra.why: The humour lives in “fourteen months” set against the outcome. “Furious” overshoots — the ACT’s tone answers stay moderate.

tone_tundra.q:
“She has read everything on the subject, and it shows in the worst way: the book cannot move an inch without stopping to cite someone.”
The author’s attitude toward the book is:
opts: critical while acknowledging the author’s diligence
tone_tundra.why: The first clause grants a virtue and the second names the fault it produced. A one-sided answer misses half the sentence.

tone_tundra.q:
“It works. It is not elegant, it will not scale, and I would not defend it in a review. But at four in the morning, with the deadline gone, it works.”
The tone is best described as:
tone_tundra.why: Three concessions then a plain claim, repeated. The repetition is satisfaction; the concessions keep it grudging.

tone_tundra.q: A word like meddlesome signals a tone that is:
tone_tundra.why: Connotation does the work: the word carries disapproval before the sentence around it says anything.

tone_tundra.q:
“The restoration has been careful, and the chapel is now exactly as it never was.”
The tone is best described as:
tone_tundra.why: “Exactly as it never was” undercuts the praise in the first clause without raising its voice.

tone_tundra.q:
“I have been asked to describe the conditions in the camp. I will describe the water supply, and the reader may work outwards from there.”
The tone is best described as:
opts: restrained in the face of something serious
tone_tundra.why: The restraint is deliberate and is itself the signal. Outrage would be stated; here it is left to the reader.

tone_tundra.q:
“There is no shortage of advice about sleep. There is, as far as I can establish, one piece of it that survives contact with evidence, and it is: go to bed at the same time.”
The author’s attitude toward sleep advice generally is:
tone_tundra.why: Almost all of it is dismissed and one item survives. That is scepticism, not alarm.

tone_tundra.q:
“He was, by every account including his own, a difficult man to work for, and the six people who stayed twenty years each said they would do it again.”
The tone is best described as:
tone_tundra.why: The sentence refuses to resolve the tension it sets up, which is the point.

tone_tundra.q:
“The new timetable is an improvement in the sense that it is different.”
The tone is:
tone_tundra.why: “In the sense that” withdraws the compliment the sentence just paid.

tone_tundra.q:
“I do not think the method is right. I think it is the best wrong method available, and I would use it tomorrow.”
The author’s attitude is best described as:
tone_tundra.why: The reservation is stated and then set aside for practical reasons. “Undecided” misses that he would act.

evidence_estuary.q:
“The bridge was closed for three weeks. Shops on the north bank reported takings down by half; two did not reopen. The council’s own survey found that most north-bank customers had come on foot across the bridge.”
Which detail best supports the claim that the closure caused the losses?
opts: most north-bank customers had crossed the bridge on foot
the bridge was closed for three weeks
evidence_estuary.why: The other three establish that there was damage. Only the survey links the damage to the bridge.

evidence_estuary.q:
“Sea otters eat urchins; urchins eat kelp. Where otters were hunted out, kelp forests collapsed within a decade. Where otters have been reintroduced, kelp has returned.”
Which sentence provides the strongest evidence that otters protect kelp?
opts: kelp has returned where otters were reintroduced
evidence_estuary.why: The first two describe a mechanism; the reintroduction result tests it in both directions.

evidence_estuary.q:
“The manuscript is dated 1631 in a later hand. The paper carries a watermark used by a Dutch mill between 1648 and 1659.”
The watermark is significant because it:
opts: shows the manuscript is a forgery
evidence_estuary.why: Paper made after 1648 cannot carry writing from 1631. It does not follow that anyone meant to deceive.

evidence_estuary.q:
“Students who ate breakfast scored higher. They also, on average, lived closer to the school, slept longer, and were less likely to hold an evening job.”
The second sentence mainly serves to:
opts: weaken the case that breakfast caused the difference
explain how the study was funded
describe the test that was used
evidence_estuary.why: It supplies alternative explanations, which is how a correlation gets undercut.

evidence_estuary.q:
“No fossil of the animal has ever been found north of the river. Sediments of the right age are exposed on both banks and have been surveyed equally.”
The second sentence matters because it:
opts: makes the absence of fossils meaningful rather than accidental
proves the animal crossed the river
evidence_estuary.why: Absence of evidence counts only when you have looked equally hard in both places. That is exactly what it establishes.

evidence_estuary.q:
“The defence argued that the letter was written under duress. The letter is nine pages long, in an unhurried hand, and contains two corrections made with the same pen.”
The description of the letter functions as:
opts: a neutral description with no bearing
a summary of the letter’s contents
evidence_estuary.why: Length, unhurried hand and careful corrections are all hard to reconcile with duress.

evidence_estuary.q:
“Every published trial of the drug reported a positive result. A registry shows that of thirty-one trials begun, eleven were never published.”
The registry finding is important because it:
opts: suggests the published record is incomplete in a systematic direction
shows the drug does not work
proves the eleven trials were fraudulent
evidence_estuary.why: Missing trials skew the record. That they showed nothing useful is likely, not proven — and fraud is a further leap.

evidence_estuary.q:
“He claims to have been in Lisbon that week. His bank shows a withdrawal in Lisbon on the Tuesday and a second in Porto on the Thursday.”
The bank records:
opts: partly support and partly complicate his account
have no bearing on his account
evidence_estuary.why: Tuesday supports him; Thursday puts him elsewhere. Answers that pick only one half of the evidence are the trap.

evidence_estuary.q:
“The survey found that 78% of respondents supported the proposal. It was distributed through the campaign’s own mailing list.”
The second sentence primarily:
opts: casts doubt on how representative the result is
confirms the size of the sample
explains the wording of the question
evidence_estuary.why: Who was asked determines what the number means. Sampling is the first thing to check.

evidence_estuary.q:
“If the theory is right, the deposits should thin toward the east. Four cores were taken along an east-west line. All four show the same thickness.”
The cores:
opts: fail to support the theory’s prediction
show the deposits thin toward the west
evidence_estuary.why: The theory predicted a change and the data show none. That is a failed prediction, not a reversed one.

figurative_falls.q:
“By March the committee had become a fog: you could walk into it, but you could not find anything in it, and you came out damp.”
The comparison of the committee to a fog emphasises its:
figurative_falls.why: Unpack the three things the fog does. None of them is about secrecy — you can walk right in.

figurative_falls.q:
“His argument is a rope bridge: it holds if you keep moving and do not look at any one plank too long.”
The metaphor suggests that the argument is:
opts: persuasive at speed but weak under scrutiny
dangerous to everyone who uses it
figurative_falls.why: The condition attached to the metaphor — keep moving, do not look closely — is where the meaning sits.

figurative_falls.q:
“The coastline here has been chewed.”
The word chewed primarily conveys:
figurative_falls.why: Chewing is slow, repeated and leaves an irregular edge. A single event would be “bitten”.

figurative_falls.q:
“Her prose is furniture: you do not notice it, and you could not sit down without it.”
The comparison suggests that her prose is:
figurative_falls.why: Two clauses, two properties: invisible and load-bearing. Choices that pick only a negative miss the second.

figurative_falls.q:
“The town had one industry, and when it went, the town did not so much decline as exhale.”
The word exhale suggests that the decline was:
opts: quiet and complete, like a long release
figurative_falls.why: An exhalation is gradual, quiet and final — the point of choosing it over “collapse”.

figurative_falls.q:
“Grief is not a room you leave. It is a room that keeps being where you turn.”
The figure emphasises that grief:
figurative_falls.why: The second sentence corrects the first. The point is recurrence, and the third choice is exactly what is denied.

figurative_falls.q:
“The new rules landed on the department like weather — not aimed at anyone, and not avoidable either.”
The comparison to weather emphasises that the rules were:
figurative_falls.why: The dash spells out both halves: not aimed, not avoidable.

figurative_falls.q:
“He read the letter twice, folded it into quarters, and put it where the light could not reach it.”
The last clause chiefly suggests that he:
opts: wanted to put the letter out of mind
was protecting the paper from fading
figurative_falls.why: Read it literally and you get the second choice; read it as figure and you get the first. The folding and the doubling-back point to the figure.

figurative_falls.q:
“The orchestra tuned, and for a moment the hall sounded like a wasps’ nest being carried across a garden.”
The simile conveys:
figurative_falls.why: Carried, not disturbed — the image is of many unresolved sounds moving together.

figurative_falls.q:
“Every map of the estuary is a rumour. The channel moves each winter, and the chart in your hand describes a river that has already gone somewhere else.”
Calling the maps rumours emphasises that they are:
opts: passed on by word of mouth
figurative_falls.why: The second sentence explains the metaphor: the maps are outdated, not dishonest.

hypothesis_hollow.q: A hypothesis is best described as:
opts: a guess that cannot be checked
hypothesis_hollow.why: Testability is the whole point. A claim no result could contradict is not a hypothesis.

hypothesis_hollow.q:
Hypothesis: fertiliser increases yield. Result: treated plots yielded no more than untreated plots.
The result:
hypothesis_hollow.why: Failing to support is not the same as showing harm. Stay exactly as far as the data go.

hypothesis_hollow.q: A model predicts the reaction will stop after 40 seconds. The reaction stops after 41. This:
hypothesis_hollow.why: Close agreement supports a model without proving it. Neither of the extreme readings is warranted.

hypothesis_hollow.q: Which statement could NOT be tested by experiment?
opts: Sunsets over the harbour are more beautiful than those inland
Salt lowers the freezing point of water
hypothesis_hollow.why: No measurement decides a question of taste. The other three name something observable.

hypothesis_hollow.q:
A researcher predicts that if temperature causes the colour change, warming the sample in the dark will still change it.
This prediction is useful because it:
opts: separates temperature from light as a cause
hypothesis_hollow.why: A good prediction is one where the two rival explanations give different answers.

hypothesis_hollow.q: A hypothesis survives ten experiments. It is now:
opts: well supported but still open to revision
hypothesis_hollow.why: Support accumulates; proof, in this sense, does not arrive.

hypothesis_hollow.q: Two models predict identical results for every experiment anyone can perform. Choosing between them:
opts: cannot be settled by those experiments
is settled by whichever is older
is settled by whichever is simpler to state
hypothesis_hollow.why: If the predictions never differ, no result discriminates. That is a limit of the experiments, not of knowledge for ever.

hypothesis_hollow.q:
Hypothesis: the lake’s fish are declining because of rising temperature.
Which finding would most weaken it?
opts: Fish also declined in nearby lakes whose temperature did not rise
The lake warmed by 2 °C over the period
hypothesis_hollow.why: The decline happening without the proposed cause is what breaks the link. The others are consistent with the hypothesis.

hypothesis_hollow.q: An experiment is designed so that no possible result would count against the hypothesis. The design is:
opts: flawed, because the hypothesis cannot be tested
ideal, because the hypothesis will be confirmed
acceptable if the sample is large
hypothesis_hollow.why: A test that cannot fail is not a test. Repetition and sample size do not fix it.

hypothesis_hollow.q: A prediction derived from a model is confirmed. This shows that the model is:
opts: useful so far, not necessarily true
hypothesis_hollow.why: A wrong model can still make some right predictions. One success narrows the field without closing it.
